lines.line: Bamboo grows slowly for 25 days, then shoots up. Which day are you on?
Like the sea, practice gets deeper slowly, step by step, never all at once.
So keep going. A thousand days of practice shape you. Ten thousand polish you.
Be like a star: never in a hurry, never stopping.
Heavy and steady comes first. Light and quick grow out of it.
Now go easy on the whip and hold the reins. Speed comes by itself.
Slow to get the horse ready, but quick to get there.
Inside, it works the same: the steadier your focus, the clearer you see.
But the pianist who rushes past the basics never plays anything well.
In Thailand we say: slow gets it done, time makes it good. Start slow.
Even the Moon rocket started slow: 12 long seconds just to clear its tower.
It's always so: every big thing starts small, every hard thing starts easy.
Top endurance athletes? About 8 in 10 of their workouts are slow and easy.
Why? A young branch falls in any breeze. With time, the tree stands firm.
Then, with firm ground under your feet, you can move the world.
That Moon rocket? As the push grew too strong, it switched one engine off.
Racers say: slow into the turn, so you speed up sooner coming out.
Same in practice: do it well first, and speed will come.
But don't load too much. Even light feathers, piled too high, break the cart.
No rush. Just practise: yoga teaches yoga, and yoga grows more yoga.
The climb hurts most at the start. Higher up, it hurts less.
So on Kilimanjaro, a guide tells climbers: pole, pole. Slowly, slowly. No hurry.
Step by step, let no day pass without one small improvement.
In time, your mind stops flickering, like a flame where no wind blows.
Once your asana is steady, heat, cold, ups and downs cannot shake you.
At the hardest spot, the master cook slows down. One tiny cut does it.
Learn it deep, practise it long, and one day a breakthrough comes.
Keep climbing, until going up feels as easy as a boat drifting downstream.
But don't run. Go wisely and slowly: those who run fast stumble.
Hokusai said nothing he drew before 70 was good. Keep practising. You have time.

final.checks:
How I built it: I took the strongest parts of both drafts. Draft B's bamboo carousel is the base of Carousel 1, because its hook is the best of all the drafts. The Moon rocket carousel mixes A and B and keeps the callback to the rocket on slide 6. The long climb carousel is Draft A's, with Dante's climb coming back on slide 8.

Changes I made while editing:
(1) I moved B12 (fast-growing trees die younger) out of the bamboo carousel. Placed right after "speed comes by itself", it seemed to argue against the theme.
(2) I put the Russian proverb C9 straight after Ovid's reins (W7), so the horse picture carries on from one slide to the next. It also gives the Russian audience a line they will know.
(3) I swapped W12 (those who run fast stumble) into the climb carousel as its warning, because stumbling fits a climb.
(4) I took W3, the Apelles painter, out of the climb carousel so it does not end up with two painters next to Hokusai.
(5) I cut the "So" that linked Laozi to the athlete numbers on Moon rocket slide 3, because it claimed one causes the other. It now opens with a question instead.

Faithfulness: I checked every line against its quote.
- B8: the rocket cut its centre engine to limit rising acceleration, which the line gives as "the push grew too strong".
- Y12: it is about overloading, so it says "load too much" and not "too fast".
- S4: it keeps "about" and "endurance".
- S1: it says "a guide" because only one guide is on record. No line claims "guides" in general.
- C6: Cook Ding slows down at the hard joint, then one slight move separates it.
- W13: Dante's "as easy as a boat going downstream" is kept.
- S11: Hokusai hoped to keep improving until 110, so "Keep practising. You have time." stays true.
- C12: it is a real Thai proverb (cha pen kan, nan pen khun). "In Thailand we say" assumes AYBKK, a Bangkok shala, is the speaker. Boonchu should confirm this.

Word count: I counted with a script. All 30 lines have 11 to 14 words. B8 had 15, so I cut "And" to bring it to 14.
Dashes: none, no long dashes and no hyphens. "Asana" is used on Y7, and "pose" appears nowhere.
Repeats: there are 30 unique ids, with no id used twice. Only one item from each duplicate-quote pair is used: C3 is in and S5 is out. C7/S8 and W16/B5 are not used at all.
Lanes per carousel: Carousel 1 has yoga (Y2, Y8), Asian (Musashi, Laozi, Russian, Thai), Western (Goethe, Ovid), story (Czerny) and science (bamboo). Carousel 2 has yoga (Y12 Tiruvalluvar, Y10 Vyasa), Laozi, Western (Ovid, Archimedes, Quintilian), sport (Seiler, racing) and NASA. Carousel 3 has yoga (Gita, Patanjali), Zhuangzi, Kaizen, Western (Dante, Shakespeare), sport (Kilimanjaro, taiji) and Hokusai.
Arc: every carousel follows slow start, then base, stable, control, speed up, and ends on the warning and payoff.
Safety: Y11 (breath "kills") is left out, so there is no frightening breath claim. There are no flood or storm images, only a breeze, a windless flame, the sea floor sloping and a boat downstream. There is no hype.
Flow: each slide 1 is a concrete surprise or a hard truth. Linking words (So, Why?, Then, Now, But, Inside, Same in practice) pull the reader from slide to slide. Each slide 10 ends on a push to practise: "Start slow.", "Just practise", "Keep practising. You have time."

verified.quote: Suppose a deft horse trainer were to obtain a fine thoroughbred. First of all he'd make it get used to wearing the bit.
verified.original: Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, dakkho assadammako bhaddaṁ assājānīyaṁ labhitvā paṭhameneva mukhādhāne kāraṇaṁ kāreti, atha uttariṁ kāraṇaṁ kāreti (Pali)
verified.who: The Buddha, to Moggallana the Accountant
verified.source: Majjhima Nikaya 107 (Ganakamoggallana Sutta), segment 3.2, tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, 2018 (SuttaCentral, CC0 public domain)
verified.meaning: Even the finest horse starts with one small first lesson.
verified.reason: Fetched https://suttacentral.net/api/bilarasuttas/mn107/sujato myself. Segment mn107:3.2 has this exact English, and the Pali root text matches word for word. The frame (2.1-2.12) is 'gradual training, gradual progress, gradual practice'. MN 107 is not in used_who.txt or used_quotes.txt. Safe content. The meaning line is faithful and 10 words long.

verified.quote: The ocean gradually slants, slopes, and inclines, with no abrupt precipice. In the same way in this teaching and training the penetration to enlightenment comes from gradual training, progress, and practice, not abruptly.
verified.original: Seyyathāpi, pahārāda, mahāsamuddo anupubbaninno anupubbapoṇo anupubbapabbhāro, na āyatakeneva papāto; evamevaṁ kho, pahārāda, imasmiṁ dhammavinaye anupubbasikkhā anupubbakiriyā anupubbapaṭipadā, na āyatakeneva aññāpaṭivedho. (Pali)
verified.source: Anguttara Nikaya 8.19 (Paharada Sutta), segments 10.6-10.7, tr. Bhikkhu Sujato, 2018 (SuttaCentral, CC0)
verified.meaning: The sea gets deep slowly, not all at once. So does practice.
verified.reason: Fetched https://suttacentral.net/api/bilarasuttas/an8.19/sujato myself. Segments an8.19:10.6 and 10.7 match the English exactly, and the Pali root matches. AN 8.19 is not in the used lists (the used AN suttas are 3.92, 5.29 and 6.55). The image is a calm, gently sloping ocean floor, with no flood or storm. The rest of the sutta lists sea monsters, but none of that is in the excerpt. The meaning line is faithful.

verified.quote: As a lamp in a windless place flickereth not, to such is likened the Yogî of subdued thought, absorbed in the yoga of the Self.
verified.original: यथा दीपो निवातस्थो नेङ्गते सोपमा स्मृता । योगिनो यतचित्तस्य युञ्जतो योगमात्मनः ॥
verified.source: Bhagavad Gita 6.19, tr. Annie Besant, The Bhagavad-Gita or The Lord's Song, 4th edition, G. A. Natesan & Co., Madras, October 1922
verified.meaning: A calm yogi's mind is steady, like a flame where no wind blows.
verified.reason: The English and the Sanskrit of verse 19 match the Wikisource page exactly. Source fix: the scanned edition page (djvu p.4) gives the Natesan printings as 1st ed. Nov. 1907, 2nd 1908, 3rd 1911 and 4th Oct. 1922. So I dropped '(first ed. 1895)': it is ambiguous for this edition and I could not check it in this session. Gita 6.19 is not in the used lists (the used Gita verses are 2.40, 2.47, 4.34, 5.27, 6.23-25, 6.35, 6.40 and 18.37). It is calm imagery and does not mock anything. The meaning line is faithful.

verified.quote: But he who has understanding and whose mind is always firmly held, his senses are under control, like good horses of a charioteer.
verified.original: यस्तु विज्ञानवान्भवति युक्तेन मनसा सदा । तस्येन्द्रियाणि वश्यानि सदश्वा इव सारथेः ॥
verified.source: Katha Upanishad I.3.6, tr. F. Max Müller, The Upanishads Part II, Sacred Books of the East vol. 15, Oxford, 1884
verified.meaning: Hold your mind steady, and your senses obey like well-trained horses.
verified.reason: I downloaded the archive.org djvu text of wg915 (SBE 15, 1884) myself. Verse 6 of I ADHYAYA, 3 VALLI reads exactly as quoted. Verse 5 just before it has the contrast, 'like vicious horses of a charioteer'. The Sanskrit is the standard text of Katha 1.3.6. The Katha Upanishad is not in the used lists. Yama is named only as the teacher, with no death imagery in the line. The meaning line is faithful.

verified.quote: Thereafter he is unassailed by extremes. [Vyasa's comment:] As a result of mastering the postures he is not overcome by the extremes, by cold and heat and by the other [extremes].
verified.original: ततो द्वन्द्वानभिघातः ॥ (bhāṣya: शीतोष्णादिभिर्द्वन्द्वैरासनजयान्नाभिभूयते)
verified.source: Yoga Sutra 2.48 with Yoga-bhashya, tr. James Haughton Woods, The Yoga-System of Patanjali, Harvard Oriental Series 17, 1914
verified.meaning: Once your asana is steady, heat, cold, ups and downs can't shake you.
verified.reason: The archive.org metadata confirms the item is Woods, Harvard University Press, 1914. I downloaded its djvu text: '48. Thereafter he is unassailed by extremes.' and the comment 'As a result of mastering the postures he is not overcome by the extremes, by cold and heat and by the other [extremes].' Both are exact. GRETIL has 'tato dvandvānabhighātaḥ' and 'śītoṣṇādibhir dvandvair āsanajayān nābhibhūyate', which match. A new passage: the only used Woods passage is on 1.20. Safe. 'Ups and downs' is a fair kid-English word for dvandva, the pairs of opposites.

verified.quote: As a result of mastering this constraint, there follows the shining forth of insight. ... Just in proportion as constraint enters the stable state, in that proportion the concentrated insight becomes clear.
verified.original: तज्जयात् प्रज्ञालोकः ॥ (bhāṣya: यथा यथा संयमः स्थिरपदो भवति तथा तथा समाधिप्रज्ञा विशारदी भवति)
verified.source: Yoga Sutra 3.5 with Yoga-bhashya, tr. James Haughton Woods, The Yoga-System of Patanjali, Harvard Oriental Series 17, 1914
verified.meaning: The steadier your focus becomes, the brighter and clearer your insight grows.
verified.reason: The wording is exact in the Woods 1914 djvu text: sutra 5, then the comment 'Just in proportion as constraint enters the stable state, in that proportion the concentrated insight becomes clear.' GRETIL has 'tajjayāt prajñālokaḥ' and 'yathā yathā saṃyamaḥ sthirapado bhavati tathā tathā samādhiprajñā viśāradī bhavati', which match. It is not in the used lists. Meaning fix: 'constraint' (samyama) means concentration, meditation and absorption, a focus practice, not practice in general. So I changed 'your practice stands' to 'your focus becomes', keeping the rest. It comes from the same page as Y10.

verified.quote: For the keenly intense, [concentration] is near.
verified.original: तीव्रसंवेगानामासन्नः (tīvrasaṃvegānām āsannaḥ)
verified.source: Yoga Sutra 1.21, tr. James Haughton Woods, The Yoga-System of Patanjali, Harvard Oriental Series 17, 1914
verified.meaning: With strong, keen effort, the goal of practice comes near quickly.
verified.reason: Exact in the Woods 1914 djvu text: '21. For the keenly intense, [concentration] is near.' Vachaspati's gloss on the same page says 'perfection is [for them] very quick', which supports 'quickly'. The Sanskrit on GRETIL matches. Note that Vachaspati glosses 'intensity' as passionlessness, while the bhashya speaks of the 'vehement method'. So 'strong, keen effort' is a fair simple reading that matches the common modern sense of samvega. Not in the used lists. Safe.

verified.quote: By yoga, yoga must be known, / Yoga increaseth yoga's store. / He who for yoga care hath shown / In yoga rests for evermore.
verified.original: योगेन योगो ज्ञातव्यो योगो योगात् प्रवर्तते । योऽप्रमत्तस्तु योगेन स योगे रमते चिरम् ॥
verified.who: Verse quoted by Vyasa (source of the verse not named, 'it has been said')
verified.source: Yoga-bhashya on Yoga Sutra 3.6, tr. James Haughton Woods, The Yoga-System of Patanjali, Harvard Oriental Series 17, 1914
verified.meaning: Yoga grows out of yoga: the more you practice, the more it builds.
verified.reason: The four lines are exact in the Woods 1914 djvu text, introduced by 'Because it has been said to be thus'. So crediting it as a verse Vyasa quotes is correct. GRETIL reads 'yogena yogo jñātavyo yogo yogāt pravartate / yo 'pramattas tu yogena sa yoge ramate ciram', which matches the Devanagari given. The same comment has the warning line suggested in the note ('by overleaping the next stage without having first mastered the lower stage...'), also exact. Not in the used lists. The meaning line is faithful.

verified.quote: Just as lions, elephants and tigers are controlled by and by, so the breath is controlled by slow degrees, otherwise (i.e., by being hasty or using too much force) it kills the practiser himself.
verified.original: यथा सिंहो गजो व्याघ्रो भवेद्वश्यः शनैः शनैः । तथैव सेवितो वायुरन्यथा हन्ति साधकम् ॥
verified.source: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.15, tr. Pancham Sinh, Sacred Books of the Hindus vol. 15 part 3, Panini Office, Allahabad, January 1915 (often cited as 1914)
verified.meaning: Tame your breath slowly, like a wild animal. Rushing it can badly hurt you.
verified.reason: I downloaded the archive.org djvu text myself. Verse 15 matches, and the OCR does read 'hills' for 'kills'. The title page says JANUARY, 1915, Panini Office, Allahabad. HYP 2.15 is not used (the used HYP verses are 1.3, 1.17, 1.19, 1.66, 1.67-68 and 2.2). 'Kills' is a classical warning to the practitioner, not a disaster or a victim, and the meaning line softens it while keeping the sense. It is 14 words, right at the limit. Bonus, unchecked by the brief: verse 2.14 on the same page says 'When the practice becomes established, no such restriction is necessary', a neat stable-then-freer line.

verified.quote: With peacock feathers light you load the wain; / Yet, heaped too high, the axle snaps in twain.
verified.original: பீலிபெய் சாகாடும் அச்சிறும் அப்பண்டஞ் / சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்.
verified.source: Tirukkural 475 (ch. 48, 'The Knowledge of Power'), tr. G. U. Pope, The 'Sacred' Kurral of Tiruvalluva-Nayanar, London: W. H. Allen, 1886
verified.meaning: Even light feathers break a cart's axle if you pile on too many.
verified.reason: Both lines are exact in the Pope 1886 djvu text, under 'CHAPTER XLVIII. THE KNOWLEDGE OF POWER'. The Tamil matches thirukkural.net character for character. The used Kurals are 415, 611 and 620, so 475 is new. Safety: the chapter is in Book II 'Royalty' and nearby verses 471 and 473 mention war and monarchs, but 475 has no royal, war or political content. Earlier AYBKK posts already used Book II Kurals (415, 620). Kural 490 (the heron), mentioned in the note, is about timing an attack on foes, so I agree it should stay out. The meaning line is faithful.

verified.quote: Will the first spoonful fill you up?
verified.original: 첫술에 배부르랴
verified.source: Urimalsaem dictionary (National Institute of Korean Language), proverb entry 첫술에 배부르랴, expert-reviewed. Definition: 어떤 일이든지 단번에 만족할 수는 없다는 말 ('nothing can satisfy you all at once'). English is our literal translation.
verified.meaning: The first spoonful never fills you. Nobody gets it all at once.
verified.reason: Fetched the Urimalsaem URL. It shows one expert-reviewed (전문가 감수) proverb entry, 첫술에 배부르랴, with the definition exactly as quoted and the variant 한술 밥에 배부르랴. The literal English is accurate, and the meaning line matches the definition. It is not in used_who or used_quotes; the used 'first pancake comes out a lump' is a different Russian proverb. Food imagery, safe.

verified.quote: All difficult things in the world are sure to arise from a previous state in which they were easy, and all great things from one in which they were small.
verified.original: 天下難事必作於易，天下大事必作於細。
verified.source: Dao De Jing ch. 63.2, tr. James Legge, The Tao Teh King (Sacred Books of the East vol. 39), 1891. Chinese from the Wang Bi text on Chinese Wikisource.
verified.meaning: Every hard thing starts out easy. Every big thing starts out small.
verified.reason: Downloaded Gutenberg #216 (Legge). Ch. 63 para 2 matches word for word. Wikisource 道德經 (王弼本) ch. 63 has 天下難事必作於易，天下大事必作於細 exactly. Used lists have Laozi 10, 15, 56, 64 and the water chapter, not 63. Laozi 64 (sprout, thousand li) is used and close in idea, so do not put the two side by side. Fuller's used 'All things are difficult before they are easy' is a different source and a reverse idea. Public domain and safe.

verified.quote: A thousand days of practice is forging; ten thousand days of practice is refining.
verified.original: 千日の稽古を鍛とし、万日の稽古を錬とす。
verified.source: Gorin no Sho (The Book of Five Rings), Water Scroll, afterword (水之巻 後書), dated 正保二年五月十三日 (1645). Original text from the Nihon Koten Bungaku Tekishu (koten.net) edition. English is our literal translation (鍛 = forge, 錬 = refine or temper).
verified.meaning: A thousand days of practice shapes you. Ten thousand days polishes you.
verified.reason: Fetched koten.net 水の巻 (三八) 後書. The page has 千日の稽古を鍛とし万日の稽古を錬とす with the date 正保二年五月十三日 (1645). It is correctly labeled as our own literal translation, and that translation is accurate. The used Musashi item is the Earth Scroll line 'studied morning and evening', a different passage. The sentence itself is about training only. Do not use the nearby lines about defeating opponents.

verified.quote: He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches his legs does not walk (easily).
verified.original: 企者不立，跨者不行。
verified.source: Dao De Jing ch. 24, tr. James Legge, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39, 1891. Chinese from the Wang Bi text on Chinese Wikisource.
verified.meaning: On tiptoe, you can't stand firm. With giant strides, you can't walk well.
verified.reason: Gutenberg #216, ch. 24 opening matches word for word, including Legge's '(easily)'. The Wang Bi text on Wikisource reads 企者不立，跨者不行. Ch. 24 is not used. The rest of the chapter is about boasting, so use only this sentence. Meaning line is faithful, 13 words. Public domain and safe.

verified.quote: Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of movement.
verified.original: 重為輕根，靜為躁君。
verified.source: Dao De Jing ch. 26.1, tr. James Legge, Sacred Books of the East vol. 39, 1891. Chinese from the Wang Bi text on Chinese Wikisource.
verified.meaning: Steady weight is the root of lightness. Stillness is the boss of movement.
verified.reason: Gutenberg #216, ch. 26 para 1 matches word for word, and Wikisource Wang Bi has 重為輕根，靜為躁君. Confirmed that para 2 is about 'a wise prince', 'the lord of a myriad chariots' and 'lose his throne' (royalty and politics), so use ONLY para 1. 'Ruler' here is a metaphor; the meaning line says 'boss', which avoids any royal reading. Not used before. Public domain.

verified.quote: ...whenever I come to a complicated joint, and see that there will be some difficulty, I proceed anxiously and with caution, not allowing my eyes to wander from the place, and moving my hand slowly. Then by a very slight movement of the knife, the part is quickly separated...
verified.original: 每至於族，吾見其難為，怵然為戒，視為止，行為遲，動刀甚微，謋然已解。
verified.source: Zhuangzi, Book III (Yang Sheng Zhu, Nourishing the Lord of Life), tr. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism (Sacred Books of the East vol. 39), 1891, pp. 199-200. Chinese from zh.wikisource 莊子/養生主.
verified.meaning: At the hardest spot, the master slows down. Then one tiny move does it.
verified.reason: Downloaded the archive.org wg939 djvu text (SBE 39, 1891). On p. 200 the excerpt matches word for word, ellipses are used correctly, and the speech begins on p. 199. Wikisource 養生主 has 每至於族…動刀甚微，謋然已解. Used Zhuangzi passages are Books VI, XIII, XVII and XIX; Book III is not used. Cautions: the cook speaks to 'the ruler Wan-hui' (King Hui of Liang), so do not mention the king. The scene is butchering an ox, which may bother vegetarian students. The slide carries only the meaning line, which has no gore. Meaning line is faithful, 14 words.

verified.quote: Whatever the Way, the master of strategy does not appear fast. ... Really skilful people never get out of time, and are always deliberate, and never appear busy.
verified.original: 其道上手になりてははやく見えざるもの也。…上手のする事は緩々と見えて間のぬけざる所也。
verified.source: Gorin no Sho, Wind Scroll, section 他の兵法にはやきを用る事 (speed in other schools), 1645. English from the Victor Harris translation, A Book of Five Rings, 1974 (in copyright, so quote it short). Japanese original from the koten.net edition.
verified.meaning: A real master never looks rushed. They seem slow, yet never miss the beat.
verified.reason: Fetched koten.net 風の巻 (九). Both Japanese sentences are on the page exactly. I checked the English in a Harris-text copy on archive.org: 'Whatever the Way, the master of strategy does not appear fast' and 'Of course, slowness is bad. Really skilful people never get out of time, and are always deliberate, and never appear busy.' Both match. A search ties the wording to Harris's A Book of Five Rings. The examples are noh chant and drum. The section's later lines on swords and marshes must be left out. This is a different passage from the used Musashi item. The meaning line is faithful (緩々と見えて間のぬけざる).

verified.quote: (So it is with) the accumulation of wind; if it be not great, it will not have strength to support great wings. ... thenceforth the accumulation of wind was sufficient. ... there was nothing to obstruct or arrest its course...
verified.original: 風之積也不厚，則其負大翼也无力。…而後乃今培風；背負青天，而莫之夭閼者，而後乃今將圖南。
verified.source: Zhuangzi, Book I (Xiao Yao You, Enjoyment in Untroubled Ease), tr. James Legge, The Texts of Taoism (Sacred Books of the East vol. 39), 1891, p. 165. Chinese from zh.wikisource 莊子/逍遙遊.
verified.meaning: Big wings need lots of wind below. Once it builds, nothing stops the flight.
verified.reason: The SBE 39 djvu text, p. 165, matches each excerpted phrase word for word, and the ellipses are correct. Wikisource 逍遙遊 has 風之積也不厚，則其負大翼也无力…而莫之夭閼者，而後乃今將圖南; it punctuates 培風背 differently, a known reading variant. Book I is not used. Safety: the sentence just before, 'ascends on a whirlwind', is excluded, and the quote and meaning show steady wind under wings, not a storm. Leave out the boat and water line. Public domain.

verified.quote: Not quickly harnessed, but quickly arrived.
verified.original: Не скоро запряг, да скоро приехал.
verified.source: V. I. Dal, Poslovitsy russkogo naroda (Proverbs of the Russian People), 1862, section 'Пора — мера — спех' (Time, measure, haste). Checked in the 1989 Khudozhestvennaya literatura edition, vol. 2, p. 71. English is our literal translation.
verified.meaning: He was slow getting the horse ready, but quick to get there.
verified.reason: The archive.org item metadata matches Dal, 1989 Khud. lit., 2 vols. In the vol. 2 djvu text (same file size as the item's file), 'Не скоро запряг, да скоро приехал.' sits just after the page marker 71. It falls inside the section ПОРА — МЕРА — СПЕХ, which runs until НЕЧАЯННОСТЬ — РАСПЛОХ. Secondary articles also name Dal 1862 as the folk source of the later 'Русские долго запрягают' form, which should NOT be used and must not be credited to Bismarck. The used Russian proverbs are different ones, including Тише едешь. The literal English and meaning line are accurate.

verified.quote: Sharpening the axe will not hold up the work of chopping firewood.
verified.original: 磨刀不误砍柴工 (traditional: 磨刀不誤砍柴工)
